description: Three example 'tasks at hand'. Each task lists the fragments (by doc file + frag id) and telemetry that matter for it, with a weight and a one-line why. This file IS the 'fake smart part' for the front-end assignment: a candidate's app can read it directly instead of building any real relevance logic. Weights: critical = miss this and you will likely build something wrong or break something; helpful = makes the work better/faster; background = context, fine to dim or collapse.

tasks.title: Bring back saved cards at checkout
tasks.story: Roadmap Bet 1. A developer (or coding agent) is about to design and build saved cards. The catch: the most detailed document about saved cards is abandoned and partly wrong, and the real constraints are scattered across payments, fraud, security, and an incident report.

fragments.match_text: If saved cards come back, they come back as PayOrbit tokens.
fragments.why: The only allowed storage approach today: provider tokens, never card numbers. Directly contradicts the abandoned PRD.

fragments.match_text: Do not build this.
fragments.why: The trap itself: the most findable saved-cards doc proposes a storage design that is now forbidden. Surfacing it WITH its warning is the whole game.

fragments.match_text: If a charge fails or times out and we try again, the retry MUST reuse the same attempt ID.
fragments.why: Any new charge path must reuse attempt IDs on retry; saved-card charges are a new charge path.

fragments.match_text: A saved card used from a new device for an order above ₹2,000 goes to review before capture.
fragments.why: Saved card + new device + >Rs.2000 goes to review before capture; the checkout flow must design for a 'confirming payment' state.

fragments.match_text: On card orders we never charge at checkout.
fragments.why: Hold at checkout, capture after weighing — saved cards change how the card is entered, not when money moves.

fragments.match_text: Removing a saved card must be self-serve and instant.
fragments.why: The customer research and checkout UX from the abandoned PRD are still valid and save redoing the research.

fragments.match_text: The lasting rule from this incident: a retry must be indistinguishable from the original attempt.
fragments.why: The story behind the attempt-ID rule; makes the rule stick.

fragments.match_text: The 20% headroom covers weight coming in higher than the estimate and small price differences on substitutes.
fragments.why: Saved-card orders with weighed items still hold 120% and capture must never exceed the hold.

fragments.match_text: Support agents see the last 4 digits of a card and its network.
fragments.why: Every surface showing a saved card is last-4 + network only; support tooling included.

fragments.match_text: Never retry a stuck payment by manually calling the charge again — not from a console, not with a script, not "just this once for a VIP customer."
fragments.why: Cards have no backup provider and manual recharges are forbidden — shapes error handling for saved-card failures.

fragments.match_text: Bet 1 — bring back saved cards, properly.
fragments.why: Why this task exists and its priority.

fragments.match_text: Never rupees with decimals, never floating point.
fragments.why: Amounts on any new payment path are integer paise.

telemetry.why: The quantitative case: typed cards fail first attempt at 9.1% vs 2.8% provider benchmark for saved tokens; plus the 38s checkout gap and 12% card-entry abandonment.
telemetry.chart_idea: Typed-card vs saved-token first-attempt failure rate, and the weekly typed-card trend.

tasks.title: Evaluate a wider delivery window for Indore
tasks.story: Leadership decided in Nov 2025 to keep the two-hour promise and fix Indore capacity instead. A developer (or agent) asked to 'look into a 4-hour option for Indore' must first discover that this exact debate already happened, what was decided and why, and which systems quietly assume 90 minutes.

fragments.match_text: Decision: the two-hour promise stays, in all cities.
fragments.why: The decision and its reasoning already exist. Any work here starts from this, not from zero — and the allowed shape is 'scheduled option beside the promise', never a replacement.

fragments.match_text: Riders, batching logic, and picker staffing are all sized against the 90-minute plan, not against two hours.
fragments.why: The real time budget: 5 min store window + 90 min plan + ~25 min buffer. 'Four hours' touches all three numbers, not one.

fragments.match_text: All batching math assumes the 90-minute internal plan, not the two-hour promise.
fragments.why: Batching logic hard-assumes the 90-minute plan; a window change means rework, not a config edit.

fragments.match_text: Indore partner stores close at 9 pm — earlier than Pune (11 pm) and Jaipur (10 pm).
fragments.why: Indore stores close at 9 pm — a wider evening window may promise hours that physically cannot exist.

fragments.match_text: When you read lateness numbers, always check which clock they use.
fragments.why: Customer clock vs ops clock differ by up to 5 minutes; any lateness analysis must state which clock it uses.

fragments.match_text: A store may reject any incoming order within five minutes of receiving it, for any reason, without penalty.
fragments.why: The 5-minute window is contractual; no product change can reclaim it.

fragments.match_text: The rider labor pool in Indore is smaller and more seasonal than in the other two cities; many riders return to family farms around major festivals and harvests.
fragments.why: The root cause is rider capacity, seasonal in Indore — the thing the decision chose to fix instead.

fragments.match_text: A rider carries at most 3 orders at once.
fragments.why: The tested ceiling a wider window would tempt people to raise; raising it means retesting.

fragments.match_text: Festival demand spikes in Indore are sharper than we see elsewhere — order volume during the main festival weeks can run several times a normal week, while rider availability (see above) simultaneously dips.
fragments.why: Indore demand spikes sharply in festival weeks while rider supply dips.

fragments.match_text: So those five minutes eat into our two hours.
fragments.why: Where the customer clock starts in the order lifecycle.

fragments.match_text: No SMS and no push notifications in that window — with exactly one exception: "your rider is arriving."
fragments.why: Later deliveries interact with quiet hours; only 'rider arriving' may go out at night.

telemetry.why: Indore at 84.2% on-time vs 96.2% Pune, with the pain concentrated 5-8 pm — the evidence that started the debate, and the numbers any fix must move.
telemetry.chart_idea: On-time rate by city, and Indore's by-hour dip.

tasks.title: Make substitution suggestions automatic and smarter
tasks.story: Roadmap Bet 2. A developer (or agent) is about to build automatic substitute suggestions. The rules that must not be broken live in the spec; the reality that must be respected lives in picker notes and incident history; and two payment rules silently constrain which substitutes are even allowed per order.

fragments.match_text: Never substitute across vegetarian and non-vegetarian.
fragments.why: The absolute line: never across veg/non-veg, baby food, or allergy items. No model or experiment may relax it.

fragments.match_text: The ladder exists because acceptance data shows people trust size-swaps far more than brand-swaps, and brand-swaps far more than kind-swaps, which they mostly refuse and resent.
fragments.why: The offer order (size swap, then brand swap, then nothing) is fixed; 'smarter' means better candidates within the ladder.

fragments.match_text: UPI orders are stricter: a substitute must be equal or cheaper, never costlier.
fragments.why: UPI orders may only get equal-or-cheaper substitutes — the candidate set depends on payment method, which almost everyone misses.

fragments.match_text: The single biggest thing: pickers do not trust the app's stock number, and they are right not to.
fragments.why: The picker is the sensor; flows that make pickers argue with the database get worked around within a week.

fragments.match_text: The rule since then: inside GreenCart, never use the store's item code as an identity.
fragments.why: Substitute mappings must key on listing_uid; store item codes get reused and will silently corrupt mappings.

fragments.match_text: Per-listing stock numbers synced from each store's billing system roughly every 30 minutes, with a synced_at timestamp on every row.
fragments.why: Stock data is a 30-minute-old hint that can fail while looking healthy; suggestions must degrade gracefully.

fragments.match_text: A substitute may cost at most 110% of the original item's price.
fragments.why: The 110% price cap, and why it fits inside the 120% card hold.

fragments.match_text: When the picker proposes a substitute, the customer gets an app notification and three minutes to accept or decline.
fragments.why: Three minutes is all the plan affords; 22% of prompts already time out to defaults.

fragments.match_text: So for any weighed item, the checkout price is an estimate, and the true price exists only after the picker weighs the pick.
fragments.why: Substituting weighed items re-enters the weighing flow; prices are estimates until the scale.

fragments.match_text: The number one complaint category, every single month, is "I didn't want this substitute."
fragments.why: Wrong substitutes are the top human-handled complaint — the metric this work should move.

fragments.match_text: It was this: stock data can fail while looking healthy, so the product must degrade gracefully when stock is wrong.
fragments.why: Why substitution is a core flow: stock can fail while looking healthy, and the product must degrade gracefully.

fragments.match_text: The one sentence that explains half our systems: trust the picker, not the database.
fragments.why: The cultural one-liner behind all of it — from a stale, unowned doc, which is itself a trust signal to convey.

fragments.match_text: No ticket, no approval, no delay.
fragments.why: Cheaper substitutes on UPI turn into automatic credits under Rs.100.

telemetry.why: Acceptance by category and swap type (size swaps beat brand swaps everywhere; baby care barely accepts at all), and where OOS actually happens (evening vegetables).
telemetry.chart_idea: Acceptance rate by category split by swap type; morning vs evening OOS by category.

telemetry.why: The cost of getting it wrong today: 9,140 unwanted-substitute refunds a month, 41 broken-rule flags.
